title: Some and any
subtitle: some friends / hardly any sugar
summary: Use some for particular but indefinite things, for approximate numbers and for unknown ones, and any in non-affirmative contexts - including the cases where some survives next to a negative word.

lesson.heading: some or no article?
lesson.text: Before plural and uncountable nouns, **some** and zero article often make very little difference: both refer to particular people or things in an indefinite way. Used this way, *some* is pronounced weakly. But we do **not** use *some* to make general statements about whole classes of things or people.

examples.text: 'Where were you last week?' 'I was visiting **(some)** friends.'
Before serving, pour **(some)** yoghurt over the top.
**Machinery** can be dangerous unless used properly.

lesson.heading: some = approximately
lesson.text: **Some** is used before a number to mean *approximately*. It is pronounced weakly here too.

examples.text: **Some** eighty per cent of all residents took part in the vote.
examples.note: beginning 'Eighty per cent ...' suggests a more precise figure

examples.text: An unexploded bomb has been found **some** five miles from the centre of Newham.

lesson.heading: some + singular noun
lesson.text: When we can't say exactly which person or thing we mean - because we don't know, can't remember, or want to stress that it doesn't matter - we can use **some** instead of *a / an* with a singular noun. The phrase **some (thing) or other** works in the same way.

examples.text: He was interrupted twice by **some troublemaker** in the audience.
I bought them from **some shop or other** in New Street.

lesson.heading: any in non-affirmative contexts
lesson.text: We usually use **any** (and *anyone, anything*) in contexts that lack positive, affirmative meaning, and to refer to non-specific, unspecified things. This covers sentences with a negative meaning of any kind.

examples.text: I closed the windows to prevent **any** flies getting in.
It was impossible to see **anything** in the dark.
We got to the airport without **any** difficulty.

lesson.note: Also with barely, never, rarely, scarcely, seldom (negative adverbs); deny, fail, forbid, prohibit, refuse (negative verbs); reluctant, unable, unlikely (negative adjectives).

lesson.heading: When some survives next to a negative word
lesson.text: We still use **some** with those negative words when *some* has the implication *not all*, when the basic meaning is positive, or when we are talking about a particular but unspecified person or thing.

examples.text: I talk to colleagues before I make **some** decisions, but I had to make this one on my own.

examples.note: = There is some person who isn't telling the truth

examples.text: I was reluctant to repeat **something** so critical of Paul.

lesson.heading: any with before and comparisons
lesson.text: We often use **any** in clauses beginning with *before*, and in comparisons.

examples.text: I cleared up the mess before **anyone** saw it.
examples.note: '... before someone saw it' suggests a particular person I have in mind

examples.text: The material felt softer than **anything** she had ever touched before.

lesson.text: A negative word nearby does not automatically force *any*: if you really mean *not all of them*, or if there is one particular thing you have in mind, *some* is still right.

exercises.statement: Money can't buy you some happiness.
exercises.explanation: Money can't buy you happiness. We don't use some in general statements about a whole class of things.

exercises.prompt: You want to say that not all sports are dangerous. Which sentence do you use?
exercises.explanation: some means 'not all'; without it the sentence is a general statement about all sports.

exercises.prompt: ___ 30% of all city buses have been found to be unsafe.
exercises.explanation: some before a number means approximately.

exercises.prompt: An unexploded bomb has been found ___ from the centre of Newham.
exercises.explanation: some + number is the natural way to give an approximate distance.

exercises.prompt: Does each gap take some / someone / something, or any / anyone / anything?

items.text: I was unable to eat ___ of the food. (= I ate none of it)
I always get to work before ___ else.
The theatre is unlikely to have ___ tickets left for tonight.
I talk to colleagues before I make ___ decisions, but I had to make this one on my own.
I was reluctant to repeat ___ so critical of Paul. (= one particular criticism)

exercises.prompt: I don't know where I got the information from. I must have heard it on ___.
exercises.explanation: some (thing) or other is used when we can't say exactly which one - never 'a programme or other'.

exercises.prompt: Elias worked hard at learning Japanese but failed to make ___ real progress.
exercises.explanation: fail is a negative verb, so any is used.

exercises.prompt: I always offer to help organise school concerts, but there is seldom ___ for me to do.
exercises.explanation: seldom is a negative adverb, so anything is used.

exercises.statement: He denied that he had done anything wrong.
exercises.explanation: Correct. deny is a negative verb, so anything - suggesting he did nothing at all wrong. (something is also possible if he is denying one particular accusation.)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make one sentence.
exercises.answer: The material felt softer than anything she had ever touched before.
exercises.explanation: We use any / anything in comparisons.

exercises.prompt: Fiona Jones is ___ I rarely see these days.
exercises.explanation: Despite rarely, the basic meaning is positive - there is such a person - so someone.

exercises.prompt: ___ parents never seem to have time to sit down and talk to their children.
exercises.explanation: Here some means 'not all', so it stays even next to never.
